workflow: Merchant onboarding restricted-business classification at a PSP or acquirer: after automated KYB, an application whose business model is not cleanly inside or outside the firm's prohibited/restricted list (or whose MCC is contestable) is routed to an underwriter, and hard cases escalate to the head of merchant risk, who can amend the versioned policy list and the onboarding rules. EVIDENCE LIMITATION, STATED UP FRONT: WebSearch was exhausted before this deep dive; every regulator, card-network, PSP policy page and press host was blocked by the egress proxy (stripe.com/legal/restricted-businesses, docs.adyen.com industry-code list, usa.visa.com, mollie.com all returned CONNECT 403 this session); GitHub code search returned 503 "authorization not ready" on every query; the mollie/api-documentation clone failed. What was reachable and read: the Stripe OpenAPI spec (8.0 MB), the Adyen Legal Entity Management v3 and Balance Platform v2 specs, a shallow clone of ballerine-io/ballerine (open-source KYB/onboarding case manager, commit 4303cd3, 14 Oct 2025), the checkout-sdk-node repo, and a third-party MCC list. No volume, review-rate, recurrence or cost figure for this workflow exists in any reachable source; all such figures below are labelled estimate or recall and none is a measurement.
geography: US and EU (France called out where it differs). The workflow is the same shape everywhere because the classification space (MCC, card-network brand-risk programs) is global; the constraints differ on the decline side (GDPR Art. 22 for sole traders in EU/FR; US political pressure on "debanking" of lawful industries) and on KYB duties (BSA/CIP via sponsor bank in the US; AMLD/AMLR and ACPR supervision in France).
triggering_event: A merchant application (or a periodic re-review / website-monitoring alert on an existing merchant) fails to resolve automatically. Concretely, in the vendor artefacts read: Stripe's account moves to requirements.disabled_reason = under_review or requirements.pending_verification, or a capability shows disabled_reason pending.review, and the outcome vocabulary is rejected.terms_of_service, rejected.listed, rejected.unsupported_business, rejected.other, or activation (Stripe OpenAPI spec3.json, vendor API spec). Adyen's LegalEntityCapability.verificationStatus goes pending then valid, invalid or rejected, where rejected is defined as "Adyen has verified the information, but found reasons to not allow the capability" (Adyen LegalEntityService-v3.json). In Ballerine the case enters the "Manual review" state with actions Approve, Reject, Ask for all re-uploads (Ballerine docs, using_the_case_management_dashboard.md). The specific trigger for THIS workflow, as opposed to identity or document failures, is that the collected facts (declared MCC, product description, website content, industry code) put the business in a category the list does not name, names ambiguously, or names differently from the card network's own high-brand-risk MCC treatment. Examples are [RECALL, unverified] illustrative categories such as CBD-adjacent goods, kratom, nutraceutical subscriptions, sweepstakes and social casinos, prediction markets, firearms accessories, adult-adjacent creator platforms, crypto on-ramps, and marketplaces mixing a restricted vertical with ordinary retail.
available_rules: (1) The PSP's own published prohibited/restricted business list and internal underwriting guidelines. Stripe's list exists and is versioned [RECALL, unverified; the page was blocked this session]. (2) Card-network rules: acquirers must assign the MCC that most accurately describes the merchant, register high-brand-risk merchants (Visa GBPP / Mastercard BRAM programs, MATCH listing of terminated merchants) [RECALL, unverified; Visa host blocked]. (3) The MCC code space itself: 981 codes in the ISO 18245 style list transcribed at greggles/mcc-codes (third-party open dataset, sourced); Ballerine's demo onboarding forms expose a 128-entry MCC-labelled industry picker for both US and EU flows (vendor open-source code, sourced). (4) Vendor-encoded restricted-industry rules: Adyen types restricted industries as capabilities (acceptTransactionInRestrictedIndustries, with Commercial and Consumer variants, and useCardInRestrictedIndustries) attached to a BusinessLine with an industryCode "for example 4431A" (Adyen LEM v3 spec, sourced). Ballerine's US demo workflow conditions document requirements on MCC: 5499 and 5912 require a cannabis_activity_license, 7800 and 7801 a gambling_operator_license, 5941 a firearms_dealer_authorization, all as json-logic rules (rules.ts and 3-company-activity.ts, sourced), and its documentation states "you can set a rule on an MCC code to auto-approve, auto-reject, or move to manual review" with an example auto-rejecting MCC 0742 (adding_rules_and_affect_workflows.md, sourced). (5) Local law overlays: state-legal cannabis versus network prohibition, EU/French gambling licensing (ANJ), pharmacy rules. (6) AML/KYB obligations (BSA via sponsor bank in the US; AMLD transposition and ACPR in France) that require the acquirer to know the nature of business.
available_facts: Structured and mostly machine-readable: declared business_type (company, individual, non_profit, government_entity) and company.structure (23 enumerated forms), business_profile.mcc (free string), business_profile.product_description ("Internal-only description of the product sold or service provided by the business. It's used by Stripe for risk and underwriting purposes"), business_profile.url, statement descriptor, owners and representatives (Stripe spec, sourced). Website content and derived classification: Ballerine's merchant report schema carries lineOfBusiness, mcc, mccDescription, contentRiskIndicators, pricingRiskIndicators, companyReputationRiskIndicators, websiteReputationRiskIndicators, trafficRiskIndicators, each indicator with name, riskLevel (positive, moderate, critical), reason, explanation, quoteFromSource, sourceUrl and screenshot; the UI explains the MCC field as "Categorizes the business by Merchant Category Code to ensure appropriate classification and risk profiling per card brand regulations" (sourced). Indicator names present in the code include Adult Content, CBD based products, Gambling, Firearms and Ammunition Sales, Nutraceuticals, Crypto, Pharma, Tobacco, Weapons and Knives Sales (sourced UI strings). Registry data (company status, business scope code, for example "46306 WHOLESALE OF HEALTH SUPPLEMENTS" in Ballerine's rule-engine test fixture), licences uploaded as typed documents, processing history where available. The facts needed for the restricted-list question (what is actually sold, to whom, how billed) are usually obtainable from the website and product description, which is why this workflow is a better fit than AML alerts; the residual factual gap is licences and undisclosed lines of business.
why_it_escalates: Three distinct reasons, and only one of them is the Sophon mechanism. (a) Missing evidence (A): licences not supplied, website empty, under construction, geoblocked or password protected. Stripe's typed error taxonomy has 96 requirement error codes of which about 30 are verification_document_* defects and 17 are invalid_url_website_* defects (my count from the spec enum, sourced). (b) Factual classification (B): what does this business really sell and which existing MCC or list line fits; Ballerine's whole merchant-report product is built to answer this from the website. (c) Interpretive ambiguity (C, D, H): the facts are known but the list does not settle whether, say, a subscription box containing hemp-derived products is "CBD" (restricted, licence-gated) or "grocery", or whether a sweepstakes model is "gambling" under the PSP's list although it is lawful locally; conflicts between the PSP list, the network's brand-risk MCC list and local law are category D. The public API vocabularies collapse the acceptability outcome into a handful of untyped reasons: rejected.terms_of_service, rejected.unsupported_business, rejected.other, verification_supportability, unsupported_business_type, plus five *_denylisted codes (sourced enums). That is weak but real evidence that the rationale for an acceptability decision is not stored as a typed, reusable object in the two largest PSPs' external interfaces; whether it is stored internally is unknown.
who_resolves: L1 underwriter for routine cases; senior underwriter or underwriting policy lead for edge cases; the head of merchant risk (or a risk/compliance committee including the MLRO and the network-compliance officer) for cases that change the list. Sponsor banks and the card networks are external authorities: a high-brand-risk merchant needs network registration, and a sponsor bank's underwriting standards bind an ISO or payfac [RECALL, unverified]. The head of merchant risk has rule-making power over the PSP's own list and onboarding rules; they do not control the network's MCC treatment.
what_gets_settled: A class-level interpretation with typed consequences: "business models with features X, Y are classified as list category Z (or MCC M), acceptable / acceptable with conditions (licence type, reserve, volume cap, network registration) / prohibited, from date D, on authority of person P, superseding version V-1". The executable payload already exists in incumbents as (i) a list edit, (ii) an MCC-to-document requirement rule (Ballerine's cannabis, gambling and firearms document gates), (iii) an auto-approve / auto-reject / route-to-review transition rule on MCC (Ballerine docs), (iv) a capability flag (Adyen acceptTransactionInRestrictedIndustries). What is NOT visibly captured anywhere reachable is the provenance layer: which application triggered the change, the reasoning, the facts that distinguish the class from its neighbours, the authority and date, and the supersession chain. Stripe's public vocabulary offers only rejected.other / rejected.terms_of_service and a free-text reason string on requirement errors (sourced).
prospective: Yes by construction, and better than in any workflow examined in the prior IPSA study: a list entry or MCC rule applies to every future applicant of that class, the owner holds rule-making power, and there is no per-case rationale mandate for approvals (contrast IPSA Scheme s.2.3, which says one determination does not bind future claims, and the SAR decision, which examiners treat as case-by-case). Evidence: Ballerine documents rules on MCC that auto-approve, auto-reject or route to manual review, and its demo workflow gates documents on MCC values (sourced); Adyen and Stripe expose restricted-industry status as typed account state (sourced); PSP restricted-business lists are public and updated over time [RECALL, unverified]. Caveats: (1) declines of natural persons (sole traders) in the EU and France fall under GDPR Art. 22 if solely automated with legal or similarly significant effect, so the decline side keeps a human-intervention right [RECALL, unverified]; (2) a settlement that conflicts with a card-network program is not the PSP's to make; (3) the "conditionally-approved" outcome (a status literally present in Ballerine's MERCHANT_REPORT_STATUSES, sourced) often carries merchant-specific reserves and caps, which are category F and do not generalise.
recurrence: Unknown; no measurement reachable. Structural reasoning only, labelled as such. The classification space is coarse (981 MCCs, of which a PSP demo uses 128; a restricted list has on the order of 30 to 60 named categories [RECALL, unverified; Stripe page blocked]). By analogy with the prior IPSA recurrence finding (one settlement per class covers 93% at the coarse category level but 37% at the fine "what was bought" level, sourced from prior_evidence.md), coverage at the list-category level is probably high, but disputes arise at the fine level (a specific product or billing model), where each new model may be seen a handful of times before either the market moves on or it is added to the list. Novel business models that need a list decision are plausibly dozens per year at a large PSP (estimate). The verifier's own estimate is that class-level H is 10 to 20% of escalations with per-institution escalation volumes of hundreds to low thousands per year (estimate, no data). Recurrence within a class after settlement is the single number the base-rate experiment must supply; nothing here can substitute for it.
current_systems: In-house onboarding and underwriting tools at large PSPs (Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com expose the resulting state through typed APIs: Stripe account.requirements and capability requirements; Adyen legal entity capabilities with verificationStatus and problems arrays carrying VerificationError code, message and remediatingActions; Checkout.com Platforms entity requirements endpoints, all sourced from vendor specs and SDK). KYB and merchant-screening vendors: Ballerine (open-source case manager with json-logic and risk-rules plugins, MCC-conditioned document collection, merchant website reports with MCC classification and content risk indicators; its README states the open-source repo "is currently undergoing a major rebuild and is not actively supported", sourced), and [RECALL, unverified] Middesk, Alloy, Persona, Unit21, LegitScript for high-risk verticals, G2 Risk Solutions and Web Shield for merchant website monitoring. Card-network programs and MATCH. Policy lists live as web pages and internal documents; rules live in the onboarding engine. No reachable evidence of a system that stores the interpretation with provenance separately from the rule.
minimal_product: WOULD DO: (1) sit beside the onboarding case manager and capture, at the moment an underwriter or the head of merchant risk decides a novel-model case, a typed settlement object: class definition (distinguishing facts as predicates over the same fields the onboarding tool already has: MCC, product description keywords, website indicators, licence types, geography), outcome (accept / accept-with-conditions / decline / route-to-review), authority, date, superseded version, source case ids, rationale text; (2) match later applications against settled classes and either resolve them deterministically or show the underwriter the governing settlement with provenance; (3) maintain the supersession chain when the list or a network rule changes and flag merchants approved under a superseded settlement for re-review; (4) export each settlement as a rule (json-logic, Marble-style scenario, list entry) into the onboarding engine so the executable part stays in the incumbent. WOULD NOT DO: classify websites or infer what a business sells (that is Ballerine's, G2's and the KYB vendors' job and is category B); collect documents or licences (A); decide risk appetite, reserves or pricing for a specific merchant (E, F); make declines of natural persons fully automated in the EU or France; override card-network programs; replace the case manager or the rules engine. The honest description is a thin interpretation ledger plus an escalation-to-settlement step, which is a feature-sized surface; the strong prior (verifier, digest) that it ends up inside the onboarding tool stands.
buyer: Head of merchant risk / head of underwriting at a PSP, payfac or acquirer, with the MLRO or network-compliance officer as a second stakeholder. This person already owns budget for the onboarding tool and KYB vendors and is more likely to ask the incumbent for the feature than to buy a ledger. Addressable buyer count is small: card-network licensed acquirers and payfacs with an in-house underwriting team number in the low hundreds in the US and EU combined [RECALL, unverified], and most of them run hundreds to low thousands of escalations per year (estimate).
roi_logic: All figures are estimates unless marked; no PSP publishes any of them. Model PSP: 100,000 applications/year (estimate, plausible for a mid-size EU or US PSP; Stripe and Adyen do not disclose). Manual review share 15% = 15,000 reviews (estimate). L1 review cost: 20 minutes at a fully loaded $50/hour = about $17 per review, so about $250k/year (estimate). Escalations to a senior underwriter or the policy owner: 10% of manual reviews = 1,500/year at 45 minutes and $100/hour = $75 each, about $112k/year (estimate). Class-level H share of escalations 10 to 20% (verifier estimate, no data) = 150 to 300 policy-settling cases/year falling into perhaps 30 to 80 distinct classes (estimate). Value of capturing settlements: (i) avoided re-escalation: if each settled class would otherwise be re-escalated 3 to 5 times a year, 40 to 80 classes x 4 x $75 = $12k to $24k/year; (ii) L1 reviews made deterministic by settled classes: if 10 to 20% of the 15,000 reviews match a settled class, 1,500 to 3,000 x $17 = $25k to $51k/year; (iii) consistency and audit value against network fines and MATCH risk (Mastercard BRAM non-compliance assessments can reach six figures per merchant [RECALL, unverified]) is real but Sophon does not prevent the dominant error, which is misclassifying what a merchant sells (B). Gross labour value therefore about $40k to $75k/year at a 100k-application PSP, before the cost of integration with the onboarding tool. That supports an ACV of perhaps $20k to $40k, and with low hundreds of qualified buyers a ceiling on the order of $5M to $15M ARR (estimate), which fails H8 for a standalone company unless the same ledger sells across other policy domains. The arithmetic scales with volume, so a top-five PSP with millions of applications could show ten times these numbers, but those firms build in-house.
review_split_A_to_H: Own estimate of the manual-review pool, no measured data; basis is the composition of Stripe's public error taxonomy (about 30 document-defect codes, 17 website-defect codes, 5 denylist codes and 2 to 4 supportability or business-model codes out of 96, sourced), the Ballerine flow in which the manual-review state is reached after document collection and website classification, and the verifier's re-estimate. A missing evidence 30 to 35% (licences, website incomplete or inaccessible, processing history). B factual classification 30 to 35% (what is actually sold, MCC assignment for known models, does the website match the declared business). C interpretation of an existing rule 8 to 12% (does the list line cover this variant). D conflict between authorities 2 to 3% (PSP list vs network brand-risk rule vs local legality, for example state-legal cannabis). E true discretion 8 to 12% (risk appetite for a large but risky merchant, reserve sizing). F commercial 3 to 5% (pricing, volume caps, conditional approval terms). G one-off 2 to 3%. H repeatable ambiguity settleable prospectively 5 to 10% of manual reviews, equivalently 10 to 20% of the escalated subset (verifier estimate). H is the highest of any workflow in the payments cluster but is unmeasured and the verifier's number is a guess.

penalties_triggered: Decision volume too low: per-institution escalations are probably hundreds to low thousands per year (verifier estimate, no data); the settleable H subset is 150 to 300 cases per year in the model PSP (estimate). Severe for a standalone product, mild for a feature.

Main bottleneck is missing data or factual classification rather than interpretation: A plus B estimated at 60 to 70% of manual review; Stripe's public error taxonomy is dominated by document and website defects (sourced enum). Moderate to severe.

Existing rules engines and onboarding tools already solve the executable part adequately (H3/H6): Ballerine documents MCC-based auto-approve/auto-reject/manual-review rules and MCC-gated document requirements; Adyen types restricted industries as capabilities; PSP lists are versioned (recall). Severe for standalone; this is the strongest penalty.

Value per decision is small: $17 to $75 labour per case (estimate); the expensive errors (approving a prohibited merchant) come from misclassification (B), which the mechanism does not address. Moderate.
Buyer unclear between the head of merchant risk and the onboarding-tool owner; the natural purchase is a feature request to the incumbent. Moderate.
Addressable labour pool small (H8): low hundreds of qualified buyers (recall), gross value tens of thousands per buyer per year (estimate). Severe for standalone economics.

Regulation constrains automation only on the decline side for natural persons in the EU and France (GDPR Art. 22, recall) and politically in the US (debanking of lawful industries, recall); approvals are unconstrained. Mild.

NOT triggered: no human-review mandate; decisions are structured (accept/decline/MCC/list entry); auditability and provenance matter; a clear institutional owner with rule-making power exists; facts are usually obtainable; no core system of record must be replaced.
regulatory_constraints_US_EU_FR: US: no statute mandates human review of merchant acceptance; the binding rules are private (Visa Core Rules and Mastercard Rules on MCC accuracy, high-brand-risk registration, MATCH) and the sponsor bank's BSA/AML program (CIP/KYB for payfacs and ISOs) [RECALL, unverified; all hosts blocked]. Whether a merchant account is "credit" under ECOA/Reg B, which would require adverse-action notices with specific reasons, is contested and PSP-specific [RECALL, unverified]. The 2025 executive order on fair access to banking and the removal of "reputational risk" from supervisory guidance raise the political cost of declining lawful but disfavoured industries (firearms, crypto), which cuts both ways for a settlement ledger: more pressure to document consistent, rule-based reasons, and more churn in list versions [RECALL, unverified]. EU: GDPR Art. 22 applies to natural persons, which includes sole traders and micro-entrepreneurs; a solely automated decline with legal or similarly significant effect needs the contract-necessity or consent basis plus safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention (CJEU C-634/21 SCHUFA broadened what counts as a decision) [RECALL, unverified]. Approvals and MCC assignment are not adverse and are unaffected. The AI Act's Annex III lists creditworthiness assessment of natural persons and life/health insurance pricing but not merchant acceptance, so a rule-matching ledger is not high-risk on its face; a PSP that also extends credit-like exposure to sole traders should check [RECALL, unverified]. AMLD5/6 and the AMLR from 2027 require KYB and understanding the nature of business, with a documented risk-based approach (H4 risk: examiners expect rationale per higher-risk relationship). PSD2 licensing means the PSP, not a vendor, is accountable for the decision. France: same GDPR position enforced by the CNIL; Loi Informatique et Libertés art. 47 permits automated individual decisions with the Art. 22 safeguards [RECALL, unverified]; ACPR supervises PSPs and acquirers and the Code monétaire et financier L.561 series carries KYB duties; gambling requires ANJ licensing so gambling classification has a hard local authority, and cannabis-derived products are subject to a specific French regime that differs from state-legal US cannabis, so class definitions must be geography-scoped [RECALL, unverified]. Net: regulation does not block the mechanism; it shapes it toward approvals and conditions and keeps a human on sole-trader declines in the EU and France.
verdict: Promising in shape, unproven in size, and structurally likely to be a feature rather than a product. This is the best-shaped workflow found across the fifteen sweeps for the Sophon mechanism: the owner holds rule-making power, settlements are approvals of business models, outcomes are structured, the class space is coarse, facts are mostly observable, and no rule mandates a human per case. Against it, every quantity that matters is unmeasured: reachable evidence shows no queue volume, no manual-review share, no recurrence and no cost; the verifier's 10 to 20% H is a guess; the public vendor vocabularies (Stripe rejected.other / rejected.terms_of_service, Adyen rejected) show that acceptability rationale is not typed externally but say nothing about internal tooling; and the one open-source onboarding tool read (Ballerine) already encodes the executable half of a settlement as MCC-conditioned rules, which is H3 and H6 in shipped code. The model economics ($40k to $75k gross labour value per 100k-application PSP, low hundreds of buyers, all estimates) do not support a standalone company. Recommendation: worth exactly one cheap base-rate experiment on a single PSP's or payfac's historical escalation log with its dated policy-list versions, coding 100 to 500 escalations into the brief's eight categories. Continue only if categories 7 plus 8 exceed roughly 15 to 20% of escalations, the PSP runs at least low thousands of escalations per year, and the median settled class is matched by at least three later applications within twelve months; otherwise conclude that the mechanism here is a versioning-and-provenance feature of the onboarding case manager and stop pursuing it as a product.
